mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office (MBIE)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path for member states: Companies Office issues original; New Zealand notary certifies a true copy if the destination requires; New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) applies the Apostille. Consular Legalization path for non-member states: Companies Office issues original; notary certifies; MFAT authenticates; destination consulate legalizes. The two paths are mutually exclusive alternatives and must never be chained sequentially.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path for member states: Companies Office issues the certificate; New Zealand notary certifies a copy if required; MFAT affixes the Apostille. Consular Legalization path for non-member states: Companies Office issues the certificate; notary certifies; MFAT authenticates; destination consulate legalizes. The paths are parallel alternatives; no sequential combination is permitted.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution and Power of Attorney
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of Directors of the New Zealand limited company
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: resolution and PoA executed before a New Zealand notary; notary attestation; MFAT Apostille. Consular Legalization path: execution before notary; MFAT authentication; destination consulate legalization. The two paths are mutually exclusive and must not be combined.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office and shareholders of the company
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: certified copy from the Companies Office or notary; MFAT Apostille. Consular Legalization path: certified copy from the Companies Office or notary; MFAT authentication; destination consulate legalization. These are alternative paths only, never sequential.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Licensed bank of the shareholder or ultimate beneficial owner
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: issuing bank signs on letterhead; authorized bank signatory is attested by a New Zealand notary; MFAT Apostille. Consular Legalization path: issuing bank signs on letterhead; notary attestation; MFAT authentication; destination consulate legalization. Never apply both paths.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory continuous screening of all directors, officers, shareholders, ultimate beneficial owners, and authorized representatives against the New Zealand Financial Intelligence Unit Sanctions Register, United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, OFAC SDN and Non-SDN Lists, UK and EU consolidated sanctions lists, and World Bank debarment lists. All individuals must be risk-rated before incorporation. Politically exposed persons, including foreign and domestic PEPs, their family members, and close associates, require enhanced due diligence with source-of-wealth and source-of-funds evidence. Adverse media and sanctions re-screening are mandatory at onboarding, at least quarterly, and upon any ownership or board change.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - Companies Register (register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Statutory names must end with Limited or the approved abbreviation Ltd; the name may be in English or Te Reo Maori, but any non-Latin script, including Chinese characters, must be accompanied by a Latin-script transliteration. The Companies Office applies a four-tier naming screen: (1) legal-form suffix, (2) distinctive primary element, (3) descriptive or business-scope element, and (4) optional geographical element, checking exact matches, close phonetic equivalents, transliteration matches, and deceptively similar names in each tier.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon rejection, the applicant may request a formal review by the New Zealand Companies Office within 15 working days by email, providing the reservation reference, a written representation distinguishing the objection, and proof of compliance with Companies Act 1993 name-availability rules. The Registrar must issue a reconsideration decision within 5 working days. If rejection is upheld, the applicant may file an originating application with the High Court of New Zealand for judicial review within 20 working days. An approved reservation may be extended by rebooking before expiry; no retroactive restoration is available after expiry.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office or commercial mailbox is technically permissible for Companies Office registration only if a physical New Zealand street address is designated for service of documents and mail forwarding is reliable; a PO Box alone is prohibited. For fast-fashion e-commerce, Inland Revenue and licensed banks do not categorically ban virtual offices, but in practice merchant account underwriters for Klarna and Shopify Payments reject virtual-only addresses without a physical operational location, local director, verifiable inventory trail, and GST registration evidence. A virtual office therefore carries a medium-to-high risk of bank denial and increased scrutiny of commercial substance.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Checklist: (1) physical signage or accessible premises; (2) lease or ownership documentation; (3) personnel and contemporaneous accounting records; (4) GST invoices and receipts matching the registered address; (5) verifiable inventory and logistics chain for fast-fashion sales. Quantified risk: unannounced physical inspection by Inland Revenue is low for a compliant digital merchant, approximately 10-15% in the first year; risk rises to 35-40% if a virtual office is used with high turnover, excessive refunds, or inconsistent GST filings. Registry inspections by the Companies Office are rare, below 5% annually, unless a complaint or money-laundering suspicion is lodged.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), particularly ss 12 (incorporation), 15 (certificate of incorporation), 16 (effect of certificate), 20 (application for registration), 21 (registered office), 22 (names), 38 (shares and no par value), 52 (solvency test), 202 (address for service), and ss 151-160 (directors duties), together with the Companies (Accounting Standards) Regulations 2014 where applicable.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Companies at the New Zealand Companies Office, a business unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), Wellington, New Zealand.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Registration of a Company (Form 2) submitted electronically through the New Zealand Companies Office online portal; an optional constitution may be attached to the application.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None required under New Zealand law. The Companies Act 1993 imposes no minimum issued or paid-up share capital and there is no escrowed or blocked capital account rule. Shares may have no par value and may be issued for consideration in cash, intangible property, or services, provided the board records the allotment and ensures the solvency test is satisfied before any distributions, share redemptions, or capital reductions.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: PRO-FORMA RESOLUTION OF THE FIRST MEETING OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF NZ_LTD. 1. Composition and Notice. The Board of Directors of the Company met validly in accordance with the Companies Act 1993 and the Company's constitution (if adopted), and all directors and the founding shareholder were given due notice. The chair confirmed that the certificate of incorporation issued by the Registrar of Companies under section 15 of the Companies Act 1993 is correct and that the Company is registered as a limited liability company. 2. Adoption of Registered Office. RESOLVED that the registered office of the Company shall be located at the physical address in New Zealand stated in the incorporation application, that such address shall be notified to the Registrar as the Company's address for service under section 202 of the Companies Act 1993, and that the office shall remain open to the public during ordinary business hours until this resolution is varied or revoked by a subsequent board resolution. 3. Share Capital Subscription and Allotment. RESOLVED that the issued share capital of the Company shall consist of the number of ordinary shares set forth in the allotment statement, each share having no par value, and that such shares are allotted to the founding shareholders identified in the share register. The Board expressly declares that the shares have been subscribed and paid for in full in cash, property, or services as shown in the subscription records, and that the Company satisfies the solvency test prescribed by section 52 of the Companies Act 1993. No further capital instalment or escrow arrangement is required by law. 4. Banking Authorisation. RESOLVED that the directors named in the authority schedule are jointly and severally authorised to open, operate, control, and close bank accounts of the Company at any bank or non-bank deposit taker lawfully operating in New Zealand; to execute all account mandates, online banking instructions, wireless transfers, negotiable instruments, merchant service agreements, and payment facility documents; to appoint sub-signatories; and to provide any indemnities or certifications required by the bank. 5. Statutory Officer Appointments. RESOLVED that the individuals named in the consent schedule be and are hereby appointed as Managing Director, Finance Director, and Compliance Officer respectively, with each such officer authorised to perform the duties prescribed by the Companies Act 1993, the constitution, and this resolution. 6. Regulatory and Dossier Delivery. RESOLVED that the officers shall deliver to Inland Revenue, the Financial Intelligence Unit, the bank, and any payment processor the certified copies of the certificate of incorporation, constitution, share register, register of directors, and this resolution, and shall do all things necessary to maintain the Company in good standing. 7. General Authority. RESOLVED that the chairman and company secretary are jointly authorised to file all notification forms with the Companies Office and to take every lawful step to give effect to this resolution. This resolution is effective as of the date of incorporation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name Search and Reservation with the New Zealand Companies Office
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office online portal (Companies Register and the 'Apply to register a company' service)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a search on the New Zealand Companies Register to determine whether the proposed corporate name 'NZ LTD' or the intended trading name is identical to or confusingly similar with any name already registered or reserved in New Zealand. Use the Companies Office online service to submit a name reservation application, select the company type as a company limited by shares, and pay the applicable name fee if one is not included in the incorporation filing. The Registrar will examine the proposed name against section 22 of the Companies Act 1993 and the general name-availability rules. Once reserved, the name is held for a statutory protection period, and the applicant must complete the incorporation application before the reservation expires. Confirm that the permitted suffix 'Limited' or 'Ltd' is included in the legal name.
required_dossiers: Proposed legal name and any additional trading name
Company type election: company limited by shares
Applicant contact details and email address
Name reservation fee payment confirmation (if applicable)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the proposed name is refused because it is identical, confusingly similar, offensive, or likely to mislead, submit a written response to the Registrar giving reasons why the name should be accepted and, where possible, provide a consent letter or coexistence agreement from the existing name holder. Alternatively, select a new distinctive name with a different suffix and re-file the reservation. The reservation fee is generally retained by the registry, and the applicant must pay the new reservation or incorporation fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation of Constitution and Statutory Consents of Directors and Shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Directors and shareholders acting through their appointed formation agent, chartered accountant, or New Zealand registered incorporation service; verification by a notary public or justice of the peace where required
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft or adopt a company constitution if the shareholders do not wish to rely on the default rules contained in the Companies Act 1993. The application must include the full legal name and residential address of every director and shareholder, plus a valid registered office in New Zealand. At least one director must ordinarily reside in New Zealand or otherwise satisfy the Australian-resident director exemption, or the company must appoint a New Zealand-resident alternate director. Each director must sign a consent to act as director, and each subscriber must sign the share subscription schedule. Passports, proof of residential address, and incorporation documents of any corporate shareholder must be certified by an acknowledged authority. The formation agent must complete the electronic Form 2 application data and attach the constitution file if one exists.
required_dossiers: Company constitution (if adopted)
Completed online Form 2 application data and statutory declarations if necessary
Signed consent to act as director for each proposed director
Certified passport or government-issued identity document of each director and beneficial owner
Residential and service address of each director
Registered office physical address in New Zealand or consent from an authorised registered office provider
Corporate shareholder documents: certificate of incorporation, trust deed, register extract, or power of attorney
Share subscription schedule showing number of shares, consideration, and subscriber names
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar queries the application because of deficient director consent, incomplete director addresses, or a proposed director who is disqualified or prohibited under the Companies Act 1993, promptly correct the electronic record, supply the missing statutory declaration, or substitute an eligible director. If the query concerns the constitution, amend and re-attach the constitution. The application remains open for revision and can be re-submitted without a new company number.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic Incorporation Filing with the Registrar of Companies
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, acting through the online RealMe-authenticated portal and New Zealand Business Number integration
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Log in to the New Zealand Companies Office online registration system using RealMe or the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) account. Finalise the Form 2 application by entering the reserved name, company type, registered office, address for service, directors, shareholders, share allotment, and constitution file. Upload all signed consents and certified identity records. Pay the official New Zealand incorporation filing fee of approximately NZD 150 using the portal’s secure payment facility. The Registrar will validate the application and, on approval, issue a certificate of incorporation and automatically assign a company number and a New Zealand Business Number. The company is legally constituted on the date and time specified in the certificate. Download the certificate of incorporation and the official company extract and store them in the statutory registers.
required_dossiers: RealMe or NZBN login credentials
Reserved name and reservation reference
Completed Form 2 data fields
Final constitution file (if adopted)
Certified identity documents and consents from directors and subscribers
Registered office address and address for service
Payment authorisation for the incorporation fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the online application is rejected or suspended because of a name issue, unresolved consent, or a failed payment, review the portal validation messages, correct the flagged fields, and resubmit. If the Registrar has suspended the application for an identity or eligibility concern, contact the Companies Office helpdesk with RealMe verification, proof of beneficial ownership, and a fresh payment instruction. Where the incorporation has not yet been granted, there is no company to wind up, so the remedy is administrative re-filing of the corrected application.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Tax Number, GST, PAYE, and Business Registration with Inland Revenue
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) through the myIR secure portal, NZBN service, and the New Zealand Business Registration ('Business Connect') facility
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After incorporation, verify whether Inland Revenue has automatically issued the company income tax IRD number using the information shared by the Companies Office. If no IRD number appears within two business days, apply online through myIR or the NZBN business registration gateway using the company’s incorporation details and officers. Register for goods and services tax (GST) if the electronic retail business will make or is expected to make taxable supplies exceeding NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period, or if voluntary GST registration is preferred. If employees are hired, register for PAYE and KiwiSaver. If fringe benefits are provided, register for FBT. Indicate the principal business activity as ISIC 4791 electronic retailing of fast-fashion apparel and footwear, and provide the expected turnover, principal place of trading, bank account details, and website or platform information.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation
Company number and New Zealand Business Number
Registered office and principal place of business address
Directors’ personal and tax identification details
Ultimate beneficial ownership declaration for tax authorities
Projected monthly and annual turnover for GST threshold assessment
Bank account details for refunds and payments
E-commerce platform information (Shopify, Klarna, payment processors) and trading name
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If Inland Revenue queries the company’s place of effective management, GST start date, or non-resident director status, respond with board minutes, physical attendance records, local agent agreements, platform contracts, and sales projections. If a GST registration is activated by mistake, apply for cancellation and provide a nil return for the affected period. For late tax registrations, file voluntary disclosures with IRD to reduce use-of-money interest and penalties.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate Bank Account Opening and Payment Rail Integration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: A New Zealand-registered bank or licensed non-bank deposit taker, and payment service providers such as Shopify Payments and Klarna under Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 customer due diligence requirements
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Present the certified corporate pack to the chosen bank and complete the know-your-customer process, beneficial ownership declaration, source of funds questionnaire, and politically exposed person checks under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009. Execute the bank account mandate and online banking terms, then open the New Zealand-dollar business transaction account. Once the account is active, apply to Shopify Payments for a merchant account using the company’s business details and bank routing data, and complete Klarna’s fulfilment and underwriting questionnaire for buy-now-pay-later services. Ensure that payment data is captured, stored, and transmitted in compliance with PCI-DSS and the Privacy Act 2020. Provide the bank with a short narrative describing the fast-fashion e-commerce business model, expected transaction volumes, refund ratio, chargeback history, and customer base in New Zealand and Asia-Pacific markets.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation and constitution
IRD number confirmation and NZBN
First Board Resolution containing banking authorisation
Certified passport and proof of residential address for each director, signatory, and beneficial owner
Company share register and beneficial ownership chart
Copy of Shopify store or online marketplace URL
Projected sales volumes and transaction values
Executed Shopify Payments and Klarna merchant service agreements
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the bank requests further due diligence documentation, promptly supply a corporate organisational chart, detailed source-of-wealth and source-of-funds statements, audited or management financial projections, and evidence of platform operations. If the account is declined, approach another New Zealand registered bank, a licensed non-bank deposit taker, or a licensed electronic money institution, and use that institution’s internal dispute and escalation procedures. Retain written correspondence so the AML/CFT compliance officer can demonstrate a fair and pragmatic de-risking decision.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Consumer, Privacy, Textile Labelling, and E-Commerce Compliance for Fast-Fashion Retail
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) Consumer Protection, Commerce Commission, Office of the Privacy Commissioner, and applicable online payment platforms as contracted parties
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Implement sector-specific operational compliance before accepting the first online order. Publish compliant terms of sale, returns policy, refund policy, delivery policy, and dateline communication in English and in any language used on the storefront. Ensure that all apparel and footwear sold electronically comply with the Fair Trading Act 1986, Consumer Guarantees Act 1993, and applicable textile fibre content and care labelling standards, with correct descriptions of country of origin, composition, size, and washing instructions. Appoint a responsible person for privacy and data protection under the Privacy Act 2020, publish a privacy policy covering customer personal data, and obtain express consent before sending any commercial electronic messages under the Unsolicited Electronic Messages Act 2007. Maintain a supplier and factory register containing composition certificates and proof of restricted-substance compliance. Establish a record-keeping system for customer complaints, product recalls, and product safety notifications.
required_dossiers: Fair Trading Act and Consumer Information Standards compliance file including textile fibre and care labels
Online terms of sale, returns and refund policy
Privacy policy and privacy officer appointment records
Email marketing consent database and consent mechanisms
Factory and supplier register with fibre composition certificates
Payment card security policy and PCI-DSS self-assessment questionnaire
Customer complaint and dispute resolution procedure
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Commerce Commission, MBIE, Privacy Commissioner, or a payment platform issues an infringement notice, complaint, or suspension notice, immediately cease the challenged representation or conduct, publish corrective messaging where directed, notify affected customers, process refunds where required, and recall defective or mislabelled products. Cooperate fully with the regulator, commission an independent consumer law and privacy audit, and agree to a binding corrective action programme. Where a payment processor suspends the merchant account, invoke the contractual dispute procedure and demonstrate the implementation of chargeback management and fraud prevention controls.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not Applicable – ISIC 4791 electronic retailing of fast-fashion apparel and footwear is a pure online commercial activity with no physical manufacturing, chemical processing, assembly, or warehousing in New Zealand; no industrial licensing board is engaged for this stage.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not Applicable – no operating licence, factory permit, or manufacturing consent is required for pure online retail. If the company later opens a physical store, showroom, or fulfilment warehouse, the applicable local territorial authority, building warrant of fitness regime, food-and-hygiene code (if any), and fire safety clearance would become mandatory.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: New Zealand Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for nationally significant activities and regional councils/city councils under the Resource Management Act 1991 for local land-use consents
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt / Not Applicable. ISIC 4791 pure electronic retailing involves no factory, processing plant, assembly line, chemical storage, or bulk warehousing; therefore no full Environmental Impact Assessment or environmental registration is required at this stage. Should the company later establish a distribution warehouse of significant scale, a regional council permitted activity or resource consent screening may apply.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not Applicable. As a non-discharging and non-emitting retail activity, no quantitative thresholds are triggered for wastewater, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), hazardous waste, trade waste, or greenhouse gas emissions from industrial operations. General obligations under the Waste Minimisation Act 2008 and local authority waste bylaws apply to packaging, e-waste, and battery returns if the business ships goods to consumers. Any future offline storage or delivery fleet would be subject to relevant motor vehicle emissions and fuel standards regulations.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not Applicable for the virtual-only retail operation. The company must nonetheless comply with the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 by ensuring a safe remote or office working environment, providing first-aid facilities, reporting notifiable injuries and illnesses, and maintaining a health and safety policy appropriate to a small e-commerce operation. No Civil Defence fire safety certificate, structural load inspection, or workplace safety approval is required for home offices or small administrative premises. If the company later opens a physical showroom or warehouse, it will need a building warrant of fitness, fire evacuation plan, Emergency Lighting and Automatic Fire Alarm certification where required, and compliance with the Building Act 2004 and approved fire safety codes.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD/Inland Revenue) is the national tax authority; online portal is myIR (myIR.ird.govt.nz). Company legal registration is through the New Zealand Companies Office (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz), an operational arm of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. Customs matters require registration with the New Zealand Customs Service and use of its Trade Single Window electronic border system.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For an NZ limited company owned by non-residents: (1) incorporate with the New Zealand Companies Office under the Companies Act 1993, receiving a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) and certificate of incorporation; (2) apply to Inland Revenue for an IRD number by using the myIR business registration and non-resident company application pathway, submitting the certificate of incorporation, constitution, registered office, director and ultimate shareholder/control information, and confirming the New Zealand agent or address details required for non-resident-owned entities; the IRD number is the single statutory TIN for income tax, GST and other obligations; (3) register for GST in myIR once taxable supplies are expected to exceed NZD 60,000 in a 12-month period, or voluntarily if carrying on a taxable activity; Inland Revenue may require an overseas-owned company to provide security or evidence of business substance; (4) for export of physical goods, obtain a Customs Client Code from the New Zealand Customs Service and, for each consignment, lodge the electronic Customs Export Entry/export declaration through the Trade Single Window at or before departure.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a check-the-box regime. A closely held qualifying company may elect Look-Through Company (LTC) status under subpart HB of the Income Tax Act 2007, but an LTC may not have non-resident shareholders, so this non-resident-owned NZ Ltd cannot use the election. Hybrid and branch mismatch rules do not create elective entity classifications; the available ordering/election mechanisms relate only to the priority of hybrid mismatch adjustments and do not change the company's entity-level taxation status.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 per 12-month period; mandatory registration is triggered once total taxable supplies of goods or services connected with or made in New Zealand exceed this threshold, and voluntary registration is available to any person carrying on a taxable activity.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, mandatory API stamping, or anti-fraud digital stamping applies in New Zealand. E-invoicing is voluntary and follows the Peppol interoperability framework (PEPPOL BIS 3.0). A GST-registered supplier must issue a GST tax invoice containing the particulars required by section 24 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, including supplier identity, GST registration number, date of supply, description, quantity, price, and for zero-rated exports the substantive zero-rating rationale. Export declarations are made to the New Zealand Customs Service independently of GST invoicing; Inland Revenue does not pre-clear invoices.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods are zero-rated at 0% GST where the supplier exports the goods from New Zealand, or supplies goods to a non-resident recipient who removes or arranges removal of the goods from New Zealand, provided the goods are not consumed or used in New Zealand and the statutory export evidence is available at the time of filing and the goods are physically exported within the statutory period, generally within 28 days of the date of supply under section 11(1) of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985. For a fast-fashion e-commerce retailer, the relevant zero-rating base is the cross-border sale of physical apparel and footwear exported directly by the supplier to the overseas customer; qualifying remote/digital services supplied to a non-resident recipient outside New Zealand are likewise zero-rated under the place-of-supply and services-to-non-resident rules in the GST Act where the services are not supplied through a New Zealand establishment or to a person in New Zealand.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Electronic Customs Export Declaration/Export Entry lodged with the New Zealand Customs Service through the Trade Single Window, with departure confirmation or customs endorsement
Bill of Lading for sea freight, Air Waybill for air freight, or courier export manifest for e-commerce parcels, showing the New Zealand consignor and the foreign consignee/delivery destination
Commercial invoice and packing list corresponding to the exported goods and the GST tax invoice

Bank inward remittance evidence such as SWIFT MT103/MT202 or a bank foreign-exchange transaction advice proving receipt of payment from the non-resident buyer; New Zealand does not issue a statutory Inward Remittance Certificate (FIRC)
Internal dispatch and order records showing the date of supply and the date of export, sufficient to demonstrate the goods left New Zealand within the statutory zero-rating period
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue may audit export zero-rating by inspecting customs export records, transport documents, bank remittance evidence and commercial contracts. If a zero-rating claim cannot be substantiated, GST at 15% is reassessed on the supply and use-of-money interest is charged from the original return due date. Shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 include up to 20% for lack of reasonable care or an unacceptable tax position, 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion or similar conduct. Failure to retain the mandatory export and payment documentation can cause retrospective clawback of zero-rating, reassessment, penalties, and in serious cases criminal prosecution for GST evasion. New Zealand has no fixed 180-day foreign-exchange repatriation deadline, but absence of bank remittance evidence is a significant audit red flag and will impair the reliability of the export zero-rating documentation.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Putea Matua) acting as the central bank, prudential regulator for registered banks, and formal administrator for the Exchange Settlement Account System, with supplementary foreign investment screening for sensitive land and fishing quota under the Overseas Investment Office
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand maintains a freely convertible currency across both the current account and capital account. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand does not impose exchange controls, mandatory conversion requirements, or withholding on current-account transactions such as trade payments, service fees, royalties, and dividends. Profits and repatriated capital may be remitted without foreign exchange licensing or prior central bank approval, subject only to normal commercial bank anti-money-laundering verification and tax withholding obligations such as resident withholding tax on dividends and non-resident withholding tax on interest. Capital-account transactions, including direct equity injections, share subscription proceeds, and shareholder loans, are also unrestricted; however, acquisitions that would confer control over sensitive assets, such as farm land or material fisheries, may require consent under the Overseas Investment Act. A fast-fashion retail e-commerce entity does not typically require this level of approval because its underlying operations are commercial property leases and digital assets. Commercial banks handle inward and outward remittances under documented economic purpose, performing standard compliance screening. The absence of a surrender requirement means exporters and retailers can hold NZD and foreign currency balances in accounts freely; no foreign exchange balance sheets need to be declared to the Reserve Bank. Exchange rates are determined by free market flows, and the Reserve Bank's remit is monetary stability, not currency rationing. Banks are also permitted to operate multi-currency accounts for eligible customers, enabling treasury managers to hedge and retain export earnings in foreign currency without regulatory friction. Overall, the regime is on the extremely liberal end of the spectrum, with only sanctions screening and genuine verification obligations serving as the de facto guardrails.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no statutory timeline and no mandatory conversion ratio for export foreign currency receipts under New Zealand law. Exporters and e-commerce merchants may hold 100% of their export proceeds in any foreign currency for an indefinite period, or convert immediately to NZD at a negotiated commercial rate. Banking arrangements may require a signed declaration on the intended purpose of foreign currency balances, and the Inland Revenue Act requires revenue recognition in NZD for tax reporting, but no surrender or repatriation mandate exists in either the Reserve Bank of New Zealand or Customs and Excise regulations. Therefore, for this turbo-fast-fashion entity, treasury policy can freely retain USD and EUR receivables for just-in-time inventory settlement without central bank conversion obligations.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Basic Operational Currency Account (NZD and USD multi-currency)
Capital Escrow Account and Business Cash Manager Account
BNZ Business Plus or Corporate FX account with online treasury portal
Business Transaction Account and FX Forward Account

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Kiwibank Limited (trading as Commonwealth Bank of Australia settlement partner)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Business Everyday NZD Account with escrow service

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Fintech electronic money institutions are viable and not legally barred in New Zealand, provided they are registered on the Financial Service Providers Register (FSPR) and licensed in their home jurisdiction as a bank or non-bank deposit taker. For this low-risk fast-fashion apparel retail entity, EMIs such as Wise Business, Airwallex, or Payoneer can be legitimately employed as auxiliary rails for multi-currency payout to influencers, unpaid customs deposits, and cross-border card acquiring settlement (especially when linked to Shopify Payments). However, a principal treasury relationship with a Tier-1 domestic bank is strongly recommended. EMIs are typically not authorised to provide overdraft facilities, professional FX hedging, or trust-grade capital escrow services. They also generally lack the physical branch infrastructure to complete complex KYC on discretionary shareholders, and their deposit insurance coverage is not provided by New Zealand's statutory scheme. Therefore, the feasibility rating is High for ancillary foreign-exchange and payment settlement use, but Low for serving as the core banking relationship intended to hold statutory capital and facilitate audited capital verification. All offshore EMI accounts should be ring-fenced, with daily sweep sweeps into the Tier-1 NZD account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical in-branch appearance is not a universal mandate for New Zealand-registered companies in the current regulatory environment. The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 allows banks to verify identity by remote video for low-risk individuals and by a combination of entity searches and digital identity verification for companies. However, if the beneficial owner is a non-resident trustee of an offshore trust, banking policies often require either (i) a physical interview at a New Zealand branch, (ii) a video interview with the entity's director and the trust's trustee, or (iii) a consular or public-notary proxy opening executed at a New Zealand embassy, with the original notarised package couriered to the bank. For this specific fast-fashion apparel retailer, if shareholders are New Zealand individuals in their own name, remote onboarding through a bank's authorised portal is sufficient. If a foreign domiciled discretionary trust is the shareholder, then an independent New Zealand lawyer must act as a referee, meet the directors with proof of authority, and certify the identity before the bank compliance committee will approve account opening. We recommend budgeting 10-15 business days for trust-related approvals and to appoint a local corporate director to expedite verification.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership sitting behind a discretionary trust with a foreign settlor, where the company register shows a corporate trustee and no natural person is obviously disclosed; transaction volume balance sheet is inconsistent with the trust's wealth creation narrative
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide an original notarised copy of the trust deed and all deed of appointment / deed of resignation for trustees, a fully completed beneficial ownership register in the prescribed form, the latest trust financial statements, a source of wealth statement from an asset manager certified under NZICA, and a legal opinion from an approved New Zealand law firm that both the settlor and trustee have not been subject to adverse media sanctions. Where a protector exists, include the protector's declaration and passport copy.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Elevated chargeback and refund rates above the bank's automated threshold (typically 1% of card sales), triggering in-house underwriting scrutiny for possible synthetic identity fraud or card-broker layering
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Dossier must include Shop Pay and Klarna raw transaction files for the last 6 months, authorisation logs with AVS, CVV, and 3-D Secure outcomes, chargeback reason-code mapping (VM, FR, services not as described), geolocation and IP hit rate analysis, the merchant's written fraud-prevention policy, and a compliance letter from the payment processor confirming no term ii suspension, plus an independent PCI-DSS Attestation of Compliance.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inbound shareholder loan or share capital injection from a Hong Kong or Shenzhen sourcing agent in the fast-fashion supply chain, triggering trade-based money-laundering suspicion due to layered intermediary invoices
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Submit a notarised share subscription agreement and resolved minutes of the NZ board, the underlying purchase contract between the NZ entity and the Chinese investor, the shipping invoice with HS codes and GLN labels for the apparel consignment, the customs entry from the New Zealand Customs and Biosecurity MPI clearance, full SWIFT MT103 with the original remitter 'purpose of payment' field indicating 'Equity Capital for Apparel Retail', the remitting bank's regulatory KYC confirmation, and an auditor's capital verification report prepared under ISRE 2400 using actual bank statement inflow.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions and adverse-media screening generates false positives for a cluster of common Middle Eastern / Southeast Asian names in customer refund and BNPL settlement pools, requiring heightened due diligence and potential refusal of high-risk patrons
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Prepare a sanctions-screening resolution report from World-Check or Dow Jones showing exact match percentages and date-of-birth disambiguation, provide the permission-based data retention policy for the e-commerce platform, submit the bank's standard transaction monitoring and negative news review log, include a board-approved sanctions policy that defines when a transaction will be blocked or escalated, and attach an independent audit certificate from a sanctions consultant verifying the true-match detection ratio below 0.1%.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: For an equity injection from an overseas parent or investor into the New Zealand operational company, the sender should execute a SWIFT MT103 with the beneficiary being the NZ Ltd's Tier-1 account at a domestic bank. The field 70 (remittance information) must clearly state 'Share Capital Injection, Invoice Ref #, Contract #' to satisfy both the Reserve Bank and the bank's transaction monitoring team. All incoming foreign-exchange wires are cleared over the ESAS system for high-value NZD settlements, while the paying bank will convert the funds at the prevailing wholesale exchange rate. No foreign exchange approval is necessary, but the bank will request the underlying subscription agreement for reporting. After settlement, the NZ company's auditor will prepare a capital verification certificate referencing the bank's confirmation of funds, the Companies Office share registry update, and any Schedule 24 foreign investment waiver if applicable. Funds should be parked in a separate Capital Escrow Account to facilitate traceability, then transferred into the operational account only after capital verification is complete. Any subsequent withdrawal for working capital must be documented in the board minutes as use of capital in the commercial supply chain.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: The principal clearing rails for trade settlements will be SWIFT MT103 for direct supplier payments in USD/RMB/EUR for garment manufacturing, through the NZ bank's correspondent network. For high-value procurements (above USD 25,000), a commercial letter of credit (L/C) issued by the NZ bank on an irrevocable basis provides supplier security, with a typical tenor of 15-30 days against presentation of clean shipping documents. For medium-value and repeat shipments, documentary collections (D/P or D/A) are advisable to lower bank fees and retain payment risk with the exporter. Fast-fashion settlement through Shopify Payments and Klarna BNPL is a separate rail: funds are collected by the payment processor as the acquiring bank, net settled into the NZ entity's settlement account on a T+1 or T+2 basis. For outbound refunds to customers, the merchant may use automated ACH/Payto rails on NZ-led bank accounts, but for cross-border refunds, a SWIFT MT103 is required. We recommend establishing an escrow buffer account with a target of 8% of average quarterly card volumes to manage chargeback clawbacks without squeezing core liquidity. Payment timing discipline should align supplier due dates with receipt of Klarna settlement funds to avoid negative carry.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: FX Forward Contracts: Up to 18-month tenors for NZD/USD, NZD/EUR and NZD/CNY, executed as principal with ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Westpac, or Kiwibank; physically delivered in NZD at maturity, no speculative contracts permitted without a confirmed underlying goods/services invoice

European-Style FX Options (premium only): Purchase of NZD put / USD call or NZD call / USD put to protect against adverse swings in payment processor receipts and supplier costs; exotic barriers and target-redemption structures are banned under the bank's non-investment treasury policy; no net short of foreign currency positions and all premiums expensed to cost of goods sold

Cross-Currency Swaps (FX swaps): Allowed for converting a temporary USD surplus into NZD for payroll and capital expenditure without spot delivery, only when the swap matures within 12 months and represents at least 90% of the notional cash flow, documented with a separate treasury confirmation and ISDA termination provision

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) are available as a hedging tool for currencies of the sourcing jurisdictions such as CNY, INR, BDT, and VND; although NZD itself is deliverable, the bank permits NDFs only as a back-to-back overlay to cover uncollectable local-currency supplier exposure, and each NDF must be supported by a sales or purchase contract to isolate speculation, requiring board approval and separate broker margin account

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (Company Annual Return) under section 223 of the Companies Act 1993
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, Companies Office, New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Anniversary rule: file within 20 working days after each anniversary of incorporation; the Companies Office opens the filing window during the anniversary month and the return is due no later than the last working day of the month following the incorporation anniversary.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing attracts a Registrar default fee of approximately USD 60/NZD 100; the company is treated as an overdue return entity and, after a further 10-working-day notice, the Registrar may strike the company off the New Zealand Register. Continued default is an offence under the Companies Act with fines up to approximately USD 6,000/NZD 10,000, plus restoration costs if the company is dissolved.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Standard 31 March balance date: the IR4 must be filed by 7 July after balance date unless a tax-agent extension applies; provisional tax instalments fall due under the IRD schedule, approximately 28 August, 15 January and 7 May.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalties and late payment penalties (NPT) apply; use-of-money interest accrues on underpaid tax. Persistent default can lead to estimated assessments, IRD enforcement action, and ultimately compulsory liquidation or wind-up proceedings.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: GST return and payment are due on the 28th day after the end of the taxable period, whether monthly, two-monthly or six-monthly; for a period ending 31 March the due date is 28 April.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late payment triggers an initial NPT of 1%, an additional 4% NPT after the first week, followed by 1% per month; late filing penalties and use-of-money interest also apply, and material arrears can expose the company to IRD recovery action.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Employer monthly schedule (IR348) and annual employer reconciliation covering PAYE, KiwiSaver and approved tax deductions
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Monthly IR348 schedule is due by the 20th of the following month; annual employer reconciliation is due by 31 May after the 31 March tax year-end unless an online filing extension is granted.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalties are applied per employee schedule; unpaid PAYE creates director personal liability exposure, late payment penalties, and use-of-money interest in addition to company-level monetary penalties.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual financial statements, audit report and shareholder approval where not exempt under the Financial Reporting Act 2013
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Shareholders and board minutes; the Companies Office only where the company is a large or overseas-owned reporting entity required to public-file financial statements
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For an audited company, financial statements and the audit report must be completed within 5 months after balance date under section 201 of the Companies Act 1993, unless a longer shareholder-approved period applies; public filing deadlines align with the annual return or the IRD-approved reporting schedule.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to prepare or audit financial statements when required is an offence under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and Companies Act 1993; directors face fines up to approximately USD 6,000/NZD 10,000 and the Registrar may order the company to be struck off.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: An independent certified audit is mandatory for a New Zealand limited company if it fails the small-company test for two consecutive accounting periods. The quantitative thresholds are: total assets exceeding NZD 20 million (approximately USD 12 million); total turnover or revenue exceeding NZD 30 million (approximately USD 18 million); or 50 or more full-time equivalent employees. The company is categorised as large and must appoint an auditor if it breaches at least two of those three limbs. Audit is also compulsory for companies required to file financial statements under the Financial Reporting Act 2013, including non-exempt large companies, overseas-owned reporting entities, FMC reporting entities, and any company where shareholders holding 5% or more validly require an audit. A fast-fashion ecommerce business commonly crosses the turnover and headcount limbs rather than the asset limb.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand International Financial Reporting Standards (NZ IFRS) for Tier 1 for-profit reporting entities; New Zealand IFRS for Small and Medium-Sized Entities (NZ IFRS for SMEs) for Tier 2 entities without public accountability; and the External Reporting Board simplified Tier 3 framework for small entities with minimal reporting requirements. All general purpose financial statements must comply with NZ GAAP as published by the External Reporting Board, and the statutory audit must be conducted by a qualified auditor under the Financial Reporting Act 2013.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a standalone public UBO registry. Beneficial ownership is identified through the statutory share register and, where the company is an AML/CFT reporting entity, through its AML/CFT compliance programme and customer due diligence records. At each annual return, a director or authorised officer certifies the accuracy of the company's details on the Companies Register, including director particulars and share structure. There is no 30-day UBO reporting window; instead, director changes and registered office changes must be filed within 20 working days of the change, and share transfers must be promptly recorded in the Register of Members and truthfully reflected in the next annual return. The substantive annual obligation is to maintain accurate statutory registers at the registered office and to provide a correct annual confirmation to the Companies Office.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book (shareholder and board meeting minutes)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 10,000 - USD 25,000 for a mid-size fast-fashion ecommerce entity requiring an audit; lower for exempt small companies

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory income tax holidays for retail e-commerce. Effective rate may be reduced by the Research and Development Tax Incentive (15% refundable credit on eligible R&D), fixed-asset depreciation, and ordinary business deductions. Downloadable software and website development costs may be immediately deductible if incurred in the ordinary course. The effective rate remains at 28% absent specific relief.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 - Company Income Tax Return, filed via myIR, Inland Revenue's electronic filing portal
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; provisional tax payable in three instalments during the year
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Standard 31 March balance date: IR4 due on 7 July following year end. Non-standard balance date: due on the 7th day of the second month after balance date. Provisional tax instalments: 28 August, 15 January and 7 May for a 31 March balance date under the standard uplift method.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Company legal name and IRD number
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Insert the legal name of the NZ-resident Ltd exactly as registered on the Companies Register. Non-resident shareholders are not identified in this field.
Use 31 March unless a non-standard balance date has been approved by Inland Revenue. Non-resident ultimate parents must align with their own tax year for consolidation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income from business - gross sales from e-commerce retailing, including sales settled through Shopify Payments and Klarna BNPL
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A NZ-resident company must report worldwide assessable income. Non-resident sellers without a NZ permanent establishment do not file an IR4. Foreign exchange gains on settlement in foreign currency are assessable.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Cost of goods sold (COGS) including inventory purchases, freight, insurance, and import duties
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only costs incurred for the production of assessable income are deductible. Customs duties and freight on fast-fashion imports are included in opening or closing inventory adjustment.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total operating expenses - platform commissions, payment gateway fees, digital marketing, warehouse leases, and logistics
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Deductible only if incurred to derive assessable income and not of a capital nature. Payments to foreign related parties for services or intangibles may attract NRWT of 15% and are subject to transfer-pricing rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net profit (loss) before tax per financial accounts adjusted for tax purposes
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply typical tax adjustments: disallow 50% of entertainment, adjust depreciation to the NZ depreciation schedule, reverse non-deductible provisions, and include any imputation fringe benefit adjustments.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after loss offsets and other statutory deductions
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Loss carry-forward is unlimited in time but requires 49% or greater continuity of shareholder voting interests. A breach of the continuity test forfeits all carried-forward losses. Non-resident equity investors must be closely monitored.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Imputation credit account balance and dividend imputation credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Imputation credits are not available to non-resident shareholders. Dividends paid to non-residents are subject to 30% NRWT, reduced to 15% under applicable DTA, without imputation credits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provisional tax paid during the year via three instalments
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident shareholders have no claim to provisional tax paid by the NZ company. Credit for provisional tax attaches only to the resident company's terminal tax liability.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Residual income tax (RIT) due or refundable
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If RIT exceeds NZD 5,000, use-of-money interest applies from the first instalment date. Non-resident shareholders should ensure DTA protection is applied at the time of dividend remittance.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late Filing Penalty: NZD 250 on the first day after the due date, plus NZD 50 per day for each subsequent day up to a maximum of NZD 50,000. Late Payment Penalty: 1% of unpaid tax on the first day and 4% on the seventh day, then 1% per month thereafter. Use-of-money interest at approximately 8.5% per annum accrues on all underpaid provisional and terminal tax from the relevant due date.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 30% non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on the gross dividend; reduced to 15% under most NZ DTAs. No imputation credits are available to non-resident shareholders.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The non-resident shareholder must obtain a Certificate of Residence (TRC) issued by the foreign tax authority and provide it to the NZ payer before each dividend payment. The NZ company must retain the TRC for seven years and apply the reduced DTA rate at source. If denied, the shareholder may file a refund claim with Inland Revenue. For cross-border interest, an Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) of 2% may replace NRWT when the lender is an approved issuer.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory rates: interest NRWT 15%; royalty NRWT 15%. Treaty rates: interest commonly 10%; royalties commonly 10% under the OECD-based DTA network (NZ-US DTA: 5% for certain copyright royalties). No WHT applies to management fees, but recharacterisation as royalty for IP exploitation may trigger 15%.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: NZD 60 million annual turnover: prepare Transfer Pricing Documentation (Local File) for cross-border related-party transactions. Country-by-Country Reporting threshold: consolidated group revenue of NZD 1.15 billion (EUR 750 million equivalent). Mandatory contemporaneous documentation for related-party transactions exceeding NZD 10 million in aggregate per income year.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not adopt Caribbean-style Economic Substance Regulations. Substance is instead tested through: (i) the general anti-avoidance rule in BG 1 ITA 2007, which recharacterises artificial arrangements; (ii) the permanent establishment concept under GB 1; (iii) the 49% continuity rule for loss utilisation; and (iv) the management-and-control test for corporate residency. For a fast-fashion e-commerce company, physical presence, local directors, employees, inventory warehousing, and decision-making in NZ are dispositive commercial substance evidence.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately omitting Shopify or Klarna settlement income from IR4, falsifying sales records, claiming fictitious deductions, or destroying transaction data for audits.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Shortfall penalty of 150% of the evaded tax; criminal conviction with a fine of up to NZD 50,000 and/or imprisonment for up to 5 years; additional fine of up to three times the tax evaded. Publication of the conviction is also common.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Under s 37 TAA, directors may be personally liable for the company's unpaid PAYE, GST, and withholding taxes. Criminal liability may be imposed on directing minds. Courts may pierce the corporate veil to order restitution.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: NZ Ltd is a mailbox company with no employees, no office, and no local management; a foreign parent exercises all substance and control, and the NZ entity merely holds contracts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Recharacterisation by Inland Revenue under BG 1/GB 1: all income attributed to the foreign controlling entity, loss offsets denied, and a 40% abusive tax position shortfall penalty under s 141D.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who signed declarations of solvency without reasonable grounds are jointly and severally liable under ss 137-138 Companies Act 1994. Courts can order directors to compensate the company for diverted assets.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Selling fast-fashion inventory to an offshore related distributor at an artificially low margin to shift NZ profits to a zero-tax jurisdiction, without an arm's-length benchmarking study.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Transfer-pricing adjustment to the arm's-length price; shortfall penalty of 20% (or 40% where the position is not more likely than not to be correct); use-of-money interest accrues from the original due date.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly execute the offshore pricing scheme face personal penalties under s 143B TAA. Inland Revenue may lift the corporate veil to pursue the foreign parent for outstanding tax debts.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Filing false financial statements with the Companies Office, failing to keep proper accounting records, or engaging in cash-intensive settlements for laundering illicit funds.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Fines up to NZD 200,000 under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and Companies Act 1994 for false statements. Under the AML/CFT Act 2009, if the BNPL or payment activity requires a licence, penalties reach NZD 2 million per offence for the company, and up to 5 years imprisonment for officers.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be disqualified from management for up to 10 years. For reckless trading or fraudulent trading, directors are personally liable to creditors for the full amount of the company's debts.
